source.title: Semantic Regexes: Auto-Interpreting LLM Features with a Structured Language
source.authors: Angie Boggust; Donghao Ren; Yannick Assogba; Dominik Moritz; Arvindmani Satyanarayan; Fred Hohman

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates descriptions generated from feature-activating examples against additional examples and measured feature activations. This is a conceptual test of explanation fidelity, but it uses SAE features rather than neuron poles.
record.gate_note: The tested units are SAE residual-stream features, not individual neuron poles. The study does not test Qwen3-32B, neuron-pole job counts, model scaling to trillion parameters, InceptionV1 examples, or attribution graphs. Metrics in Table A1 evaluate descriptions on examples or generated text; faithfulness results concern steered generations and are not included as rows for V6. The table reports means over 100 randomly selected features per layer for each feature set, rather than per-feature good-score fractions. User-study findings are included as a separate aggregate result.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It benchmarks its semantic-regex description format against two natural-language description methods (token-act-pair, max-acts) on SAE residual-stream features of GPT-2-Small and Gemma-2-2B. It reports its own method's performance relative to these baselines. It does not measure how well individual neurons or neuron poles are explained, and it is not framed around whether activating-example explanations overstate interpretability. The units are SAE latents, not neurons. So no row measures what any version names (neurons, by the same kind of unit). The record's T2 and V6 links are wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that semantic regexes match natural-language accuracy while being more concise and consistent. They add that the structure lets feature complexity be read across layers, with complexity increasing with depth, and that semantic regexes help people build accurate mental models. They note terseness, non-uniqueness, ambiguity and polysemanticity as limitations.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an automated feature-description pipeline and SAE latent features, not a neuron-pole audit or the original neuron explanation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Description format and evaluation metric vary; the authors also report that GPT-4o versus GPT-4o-mini does not change relative performance in their 520-feature ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: For SAE features, descriptions generated from top activating examples generate activating text much less reliably than they discriminate known examples. Token-act-pair clarity is 0.25–0.45, against detection of 0.77–0.79, and clarity falls with the larger 65k dictionary. GPT-4o in place of GPT-4o-mini lifts token-act-pair clarity from 0.45 to 0.59.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For SAE latents, activating-example descriptions overstate how well a description predicts which new text activates the latent. The gap depends on description method and dictionary size.

record.problems: The measured units are SAE features rather than neurons. Main quantitative results are aggregates over sampled features per layer and do not report the share of individual features passing a good-score threshold. Evaluations rely on GPT-4o-mini as evaluator except for the stated model ablation; the authors note that existing discrete evaluator metrics can yield false positives and false negatives.
record.rows_left_out: Faithfulness scores were omitted because they score steered generations against feature descriptions rather than testing prediction of feature firing on new text. Other user-study details are qualitative and not separately quantified in the text.

untested.parts: Neuron interpretability shares across dense/MoE models and scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and recursive generalization.
Architecture/regularization/tool effects on the share of interpretable neurons.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
Whether neuron explanations fitting activating examples fail to predict firing; only SAE features are studied.
Fraction of neurons with good simulation scores, and the effect of stronger explainers on neuron scores.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are all method-benchmark scores on SAE latents: the study's own method plus two baselines. The units are SAE latents, not neurons, and the study is not one of the original sources. The authors state that they focus on SAE features rather than neurons. Means over 100 features per layer give no per-feature pass rate, so V7 can't be read even by analogy.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and the reported shares of one job, two related jobs, and not-yet-understood poles.
Neuron interpretability shares across models, architectures, and trillion-parameter scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and the recursive-generalization account.
Architecture, regularization, tool quality, and the stated InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and reconstruction error.
The study tests SAE feature descriptions, not neuron explanations specifically; it does not isolate descriptions that fit their source examples and then measure where the same neuron fires.
The study does not report the fraction of neurons receiving good automated scores, and does not compare such fractions across explainer models.

rows.subject: GPT-2-RES-25k
rows.operation_detail: Participants generated positive phrases and counterfactuals from feature descriptions; the subject feature's activations were compared.
rows.measure: Features where participant performance using semantic-regex was as good as or higher than max-acts
rows.baseline: max-acts descriptions of the same features
rows.note: The paper says natural language substantially outperformed semantic-regex on two features; the semantic regexes were accurate but too minimal to elicit strongly activating phrases.
rows.check: User study on 12 hand-selected SAE features pre-filtered for detection above 75%. It compares the study's own format against max-acts and does not measure neuron explanation fidelity.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: User-study features where terse semantic-regex descriptions elicited weaker activating phrases
reader_labels.reason: The authors report two features where natural-language descriptions substantially outperformed semantic-regex descriptions, because the latter were too minimal; row u1.
